## Intent
Hypothesis: a Halide-expressible branchless blend formulation of the integrate-decide-respawn loop can eliminate death-rate sensitivity and approach the streaming ceiling.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout at 68 B/particle offers loop 1 only 32 hot bytes (47% — age+pos+seed+vel) and loop 2 only 28 hot bytes (41% — color+pos), so 53–59% of each cacheline fill is dead weight dragged through the line filler. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers — no extra bandwidth for respawn decisions. The branchless blend approach (per-particle hash RNG, `csel`-based respawn) is designed to avoid branch misprediction when death rates climb. The working set spills L1d at N≈963 and L2 at N≈61680; with only 47% hot bytes the effective hot footprint is smaller, but the dead-weight bytes still consume cache capacity since the 128-byte line filler drags all 68 bytes per particle regardless.

## Cache saturation
The ns/particle curve is strikingly flat across all regimes: ~8.3 ns/p in L1d (N=380–960), ~8.0 ns/p in L2 (N=1400–41000), and ~7.6 ns/p in DRAM (N=62000+). There is no spill knee — cost actually *decreases* slightly moving from L1d to DRAM, the signature of a compute-bound kernel where cache residency is irrelevant. The 53% dead-weight fraction would normally cause a bandwidth penalty at the L2→DRAM transition, but since achieved bandwidth is only ~30% of ceiling, the prefetcher has ample headroom to hide the wasted bytes. The dense grid confirms no cache-dependent behavior at any transition.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth holds at 8.0–9.1 GB/s across all N and q — roughly 27–30% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling and 3.3–3.7× above the 2.274 ns/p memory floor. The algo is firmly compute-bound: at N=10000/q=0.01, compute is 76.8% with only 15.2% backend stall; at N=1000000/q=0.5, compute rises to 88.8%. The death-rate effect is the dominant axis: at q=0.01 the algo is 1.03–1.16× *slower* than naive scalar (the `bl _halide_b2` call overhead and scalar render add cost when few particles die), but at q=0.5 it drops to 0.56× baseline — the branchless blend pays off when half the particles respawn. Against the winner, the gap narrows from 2.3× at q=0.01/N=380 to 1.4× at q=0.5 but never closes, because the winner pairs halide loop 1 with an optimized render (LP2-opt) that this cell lacks.

## Assembly
The codegen reveals why this never approaches the ceiling: the step function delegates the main computation to `_halide_b2` via `bl` (an external AOT call), and the inlined render loop is entirely scalar. Only 2 of 354 instructions are vector-suffixed (both `movi.2d` for register zeroing) — no SIMD on particle data whatsoever. The loop digest shows ~147 insns/iter with 15 conditional branches, `csel` ×18 for the death verdict (branchless blend as intended), but `strb` ×16 for byte-granular pixel scatter and scalar FP (`fmul`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fcvtzs`) ×17. The render loop does `ldrb`/`strb` pairs with `csel` clamping to 0xFF — three byte stores per particle with no vectorization. The scalar FP and byte-scatter explain the 76–89% compute fraction; the absence of SIMD explains why bandwidth sits at 30% of ceiling despite the streaming-friendly stride-68 access pattern.

## Verdict
Partially holds — the branchless blend does flatten performance across N (no cache-spill knee, 7.5–8.5 ns/p everywhere) and at q=0.5 the algo runs at 0.56× baseline (1.7× faster than naive). But the hypothesis of approaching the streaming ceiling is refuted: 3.3–3.7× above the memory floor, only 30% of ceiling, and 1.4–2.3× slower than the winner at every N×q point. The mechanism is the codegen: the halide schedule delegates to an external AOT call and leaves the render loop as scalar FP with byte-granular `strb` scatter — 2 vector instructions in 354 — so the branchless blend saves branch flushes (0.5–3.6%) but cannot overcome the compute cost of unvectorized arithmetic.
